It has been revealed that as someone who leads a busy, on-the-go lifestyle and travels a lot, I've never utilized a massage gun as much as this compact one. Its scaled-down size and lightweight design make it practical to chuck in my carry-on, backpack, or gym/work bag, so I bring it out of the house with me nearly every day.

Despite its smaller size, this massage gun's performance stands out, delivering a powerful massage experience that's comparable to its larger counterparts. It weighs less than 1.5 pounds, has 150 minutes of battery life, three different speed settings, and three attachment heads, so you're not missing out on much that bigger models may offer. I will say, however, it does deliver a slightly more surface-level massage than the Theragun PRO (which I used before acquiring the Mini). That being noted, the power and depth offered by the Mini is plenty for most people to reap the benefits of percussion therapy.

"This is hands-down my favorite massage gun. its small enough that I can travel with it anywhere, and despite its odd shape, I find it easy to hold and use," says Samuel. "It’s my go-to for loosening chest and IT bands.".

In a recent development, for those interested in adding a few premium features, I've also tested the Theragun Mini Plus, which provides heat to the treatment area. And regardless of the need for heat application for better recovery in your case, it does provide a pleasant experience. I wouldn’t say it is necessary for the price, and this original design can’t be beat.

My only qualm with this thing is that it's noise level is a limiting factor in terms of where I actually use it. It's compact and lightweight enough to bring on-the-go, but it's definitely not quiet enough to use in a subdued office setting, for example. It's quieter than larger models, but not as dampened as you'd think for one so small.

Read More: Theragun Mini Review.

It has been revealed that this massage gun from Renpho is one of the most popular purchases on Amazon and we can see why. With four interchangeable massage heads and five speed settings, this sub-$100 device competes with the likes of Hyperice and Therabody for pennies on the dollar.

Sources indicate that featuring a minimalist, ergonomic design, this massage gun feels comfortable and manageable in my hand, targeting everything from my traps to calves. The motor is powerful, delivering a massage that falls somewhere between the Hypervolt 3 and the Theragun PRO in terms of intensity.

Its battery life also impressed me, but the charging itself took a little bit longer than other models on the market. Whether you're looking for an entry-level massage gun to test the waters or want to purchase a spare to leave at the office, this one is a no-brainer in terms of overall value.

For anyone looking for a suitably powerful and quiet full-sized model, this is the way to go. Sure, there is the standard Hypervolt 3, but for a little more money, you can get two additional power settings, which means more options when it comes to your treatment. And if you want something that packs slightly less of a punch and is more mobile, the Hypervolt 3 Go is a much better pick.

The max power level on this gun is less than others on the list, but I don't count that as a negative. Instead, the additional power settings allow you to access lower levels than other devices, which will be welcomed by many customers like me.

According to recent reports, for the variability and the performance that this massage gun delivers, the weight is very reasonable. The handle is easy to grip and gives you good stability when you want to dig into the muscles a little deeper.

Read More: Normatec Elite Compression Boots Review.

In a recent development, the Theragun Prime Plus includes a 120-minute battery life, heated attachment, and a multi-grip handle that makes hard-to-reach areas more accessible. There are quite a few Theraguns on the market right now, and I've tested them all. Choosing between the many full-sized options can be difficult, but in my opinion, this is the standout amongst the crowd.

Sources indicate that for the percussive force it distributes, the weight is surprisingly light. The unique design allows me to change up my grip however I wish. And unlike other premium options, it's light enough for you to actually handle it with each grip. The heated attachment provides comfort during your treatment, and while its warmth may not actually be scientifically proven to be effective in this application, it is pleasant during use.

According to recent reports, like the other higher-end Theragun models, the Prime Plus also has “smart” capabilities with the Therabody app, which allows users to track progress and data with Bluetooth connectivity. With four attachments, plus five different percussion settings with up to 60 pounds of force, this massager leaves nothing to be desired.

Recent findings suggest that ekrin has entered the world of massage gun devices and quickly made a noticeable splash. This powerful massager has a sleekly designed handle that looks basic but more than gets the job done. It's easy to use, and comes with six different massage heads to target muscle groups in different ways.

Our Health Director Marty Munson finds the ergonomic design impressive. "I have joint issues in my hands, but this grip is really comfortable," says Munson. "I've used many of the mainstay models out there, but I'm impressed with how good this one is.".

The device also has six different speed settings and a rechargeable battery, which provides up to 8 hours of use on a single charge. It also delivers up to 3,500 percussions per minute, meaning it's a good option if power is toward the top of your massage gun must-haves list.

The Rally Orbital Massager stands out as a versatile and effective new tool in recovery, which is why it earned a spot in our Men’s Health Fitness Awards. Its ergonomic design fits comfortably in the hand, making it easy to maneuver across different muscle groups. The device offers multiple intensity levels, allowing you to customize the massage experience based on your specific needs, whether it’s for post-workout recovery or general tension relief.

Industry observers note that samuel is a fan, finding this device gentler than other options and perhaps more appropriate for a larger segment of the population. Even at higher intensities, the device operates with minimal noise, making it suitable for use in shared spaces or while watching TV. The battery life is also pretty solid.

Industry observers note that overall, the Rally Orbital Massager delivers excellent value for anyone seeking an accessible at-home massage solution, and manages to bring more innovation to a space that has been advancing for years. Its combination of thoughtful design, strong performance, and user-friendly features makes it a standout choice among other premium products.

In a recent development, to learn more about what to look for in a massage gun, we spoke with Vinh Pham, PT, a physical therapist and the founder of Myodetox, a manual therapy and movement clinic with locations in Canada and the U.S. According to Pham, the three most notable things are reliability, noise, and battery life. "I need something that I know is well-made and won’t malfunction during operation, especially because I’m using it on injured athletes. Noise is the next most important factor. I need to be able to talk to my athletes over the noise of the gun without yelling at them.".

Keeping treatment quiet is a major priority. "Personally, noise to me is number one," claims Pham. "I want to be able to use the massage guns in public, and having it sound like a power tool would make it unusable." This is a feeling that I also agree with; especially when treating yourself around other people, you can feel self-conscious.

Sources indicate that next up is battery life, as PTs and athletes can’t have guns dying in the middle of treatment. Pham claims that he expects a massage gun to last several full days without requiring a charge. "You’ll also want to be able to throw the gun in your bag or take it on a weekend trip without worrying about finding an outlet," Pham says.

Recent findings suggest that given the fact that massage guns are required to vibrate intensely in order to get the job done, it's not the kind of product you want to be sent with loose screws. Given how much the market has grown in recent years, there have been a lot of knockoff brands releasing subpar models that won't go the distance. Hands-on experience, like our team at Men's Health focuses on, is key in the research process. All of our picks have been vetted for durability, but it comes as no surprise that if you want the best and a brand name you can trust, you should expect to spend a little more.

Industry observers note that sufficient speed, or percussions per minute (PPM), plays a role in how the gun promotes blood flow. The higher the percussive rate, the more it can stimulate circulation. Look for a massage gun with a high percussive force and adjustable speed settings so you can deliver adequate force to different muscles. Another factor to consider is amplitude, which describes the amount of distance the massage head travels back and forth. This controls how effectively you can target certain muscle groups and how deeply the massager can get into the muscle tissue.

In a recent development, just as notable as amplitude is the gun's stall force, or the amount of pressure that the motor can apply to the muscle before it stops working. The higher the stall force, the more powerful a massage the gun can put out. Remember, though, that a massage gun shouldn't necessarily attack your muscles. In fact, for most people, less force is more. So don't get overly caught up in having the most "powerful" gun on the market; you likely won't need it to gain recovery benefits.

Different attachments can provide different massage techniques and sensations that may be suitable for different muscles. Many massage guns tout a host of attachments, but realize this: You'll likely just use a handful of these (or sometimes, your favorite one). So don't get deluded into purchasing because of multiple attachments. Once you've purchased your massage gun, be sure to properly research what attachments are effective for what muscles. Using the wrong attachment can dramatically alter the effectiveness of the massage gun.

A portable and lightweight massage gun is ideal, especially if you plan to use it on the go or travel with it. Consider the weight, size, and the case included.

Of course, even the best guns leave room for improvement. Some options come with convenient travel cases and charging stands—something Pham would like to see more products offer. He also mentions that dishwasher-safe attachment heads would make for easier cleaning. And, as the market continues to progress, he hopes for smaller (yet still powerful) designs and Bluetooth app integration.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, part of my job is to evaluate the latest and greatest recovery gear available. I've used massage guns regularly for the past decade for muscle activation and post-training recovery. The testing pool for this list started with dozens of models across a range of price points, including the bestselling brands, both established and upcoming. I tested each for several weeks, in multiple scenarios, including at home and at the gym.

In addition to my own testing, this guide was made with input and testing notes from other knowledgeable Men's Health editors, including MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. We consulted with respected physical therapists like Vinh Pham, PT, at Myodetox and Renato Sanchez for expert advice. We evaluated each device for durability, effectiveness, ergonomics (for ease of use), and portability. We also considered price point, as many massage guns offer better overall value than others.

After all this testing and research, we found these massage guns that we recommend.

Sanchez recommends first asking yourself why you’re considering a massage gun. "What are you looking to get out of one? Is it for recovery, pain relief, or helping you reach your fitness goals? If you answered yes to any of those, then you might be a good candidate to add one to your shopping cart," he explains.

Industry observers note that "Massage guns can be used as an alternative to the foam roller as a self-myofascial release tool," adds Pham. He notes that benefits include everything from decreased stress, pain, and tissue tension to enhanced recovery, blood circulation, and range of motion.

"You can use it pre-workout to warm up the muscles and post-workout to decrease tightness and soreness," says Pham.

In a recent development, you don’t want to spend hours upon hours using your massage gun. Instead, you’ll want to spend 90 to 120 seconds on any given muscle group, floating the gun across that area, according to Samuel. "Aim to follow the direction of the muscle fibers. That means running your gun across your chest, from the center toward your shoulder, instead of running it up and down your chest.".

But be mindful to not run your massage gun across joints; you want to keep it focused on the soft tissue only. "And don’t try to aggressively drive the gun deep into the muscle, expecting more 'relief.' Using a massage gun shouldn’t hurt," explains Samuel.

Recent findings suggest that want to learn more on how you should be using one of these buzzy tools? Check out our how-to-use massage guns guide for instructions for best practices before, during, and after workouts.

Massage guns have gained a lot of popularity in recent years as a tool for muscle recovery—but do they really work? The blunt answer is they can. But it all depends on how, when, and where you use them.

In a recent development, these massagers offer rapid, percussive strokes designed to penetrate the muscle tissue, stimulate blood flow, and help break up adhesions. The research on the effectiveness of massage guns for muscle recovery is promising, but still limited.

According to recent reports, A study published in the Journal of Clinical and Diagnostic Research found that using a massage gun on the quadriceps muscles after exercise resulted in a significant reduction in muscle soreness and an increase in muscle flexibility compared to a control group. Another study found that using a massage gun after exercise improved blood flow to the muscles and reduced muscle fatigue.

So, they can help with muscle soreness with correct use, but shouldn't be used as a replacement for other recovery methods such as rest, proper nutrition, active stretching, and dynamic mobility work.

We asked Sanchez how folks can get to those hard-to-reach areas with their massage guns. Here's his take: "Massage guns mainly target superficial muscles making it hard to isolate deeper musculature. Therefore, yes, the location of muscles can impact the effectiveness of this modality.

I think it’s safe to say the majority of people can reach the front side of their bodies using a massage gun, but you’ll need decent shoulder mobility if you’re looking to target the mid and low back. That’s when you’d want to get a massage gun that is more ergonomic or can be adjusted.

Industry observers note that if mobility is a limiting factor, you may consider trading the massage gun for a lacrosse ball for pinpoint contact. Sometimes you might just be better off asking a friend, what’s the saying … I’ll scratch your back if you scratch mine?".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

In a recent development, the key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

It has been revealed that that personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk stated the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

According to recent reports, you don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if customers join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

In a recent development, and the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no newly introduced revenue attached.

Recent findings suggest that A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

According to recent reports, huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

It has been revealed that the Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” stated Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”.

Sources indicate that huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It’s easy to underrate walking as one of the best things we can do for our fitness—after all, it doesn’t get your heart rate up like running or a HIIT workout.
  • Recent findings suggest that and perhaps one of the best things about walking is that it doesn’t require any specialized equipment or gear except a really good pair of comfy walking shoes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s easy to underrate walking as one of the best things we can do for our fitness—after all, it doesn’t get your heart rate up like running or a HIIT workout. But that doesn’t mean you’re not getting tons of physical and mental health benefits from walking, whether you’re following a walking workout blueprint or not.

Recent findings suggest that and perhaps one of the best things about walking is that it doesn’t require any specialized equipment or gear except a really good pair of comfy walking shoes. Luckily for you, we’re constantly testing walking shoes, and we’ve narrowed down all the options out there to a list of pairs we reach for again and again. We’ve used our testing experience, plus picked the brains of podiatrists and other experts to compile our favorites in this guide.

If you’ve logged even a couple of miles in a not-so-great pair of walking shoes, you know wearing the wrong footwear can make what started out as a nice walk turn into an uncomfortable slog fast (we’re talking blisters, achy arches, plantar fasciitis, and more).

Industry observers note that the right walking shoes, on the other hand, can help you walk farther, feel happier while doing it, and gush to friends about your sneakers (ask us how we know). Plus, select styles can help prevent injury or overpronation (when your arches collapse and cause your foot to angle inward), indicates podiatrist Chanel Perkins, DPM, an assistant professor of foot and ankle podiatry in the Department of Orthopedic Surgery and Rehabilitation at the University of Texas Medical Branch.

It has been revealed that after testing dozens of walking shoes for our 2026 Fitness Awards, the Adrenaline GTS 25 took the top spot for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. Our staffers who tested it say it’s comfortable enough to walk in for hours. “It offers just the right amount of cushioning for a bouncy step without compromising on support for my flat, wide feet,” indicates WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders.

That comfort starts with the 25’s updated midsole, which feels plusher than previous models without losing an ounce of stability. It still features the brand’s signature GuardRails technology—firmer along the sides and softer through the center—to gently lock in your stride. In our testing, Brooks continues to set the standard for stability, making this a standout pick for anyone whose feet tend to roll inward while walking.

Sources indicate that when it comes to fit, the 25 has a roomier toe box up front and a secure (but still comfortable) heel lock back, which helps cut down on friction and lowers your chances of blisters during long walks. The higher 10 mm drop creates a slightly forward-leaning stride that takes pressure off the calves and Achilles, making the 25 a smart pick for anyone with tight lower legs or Achilles sensitivity. If you prefer a flatter feel underfoot, though, we recommend something lower profile like the Hoka Mach 6.

At 9.5 ounces, it’s one of the heavier options on this list, but that added weight comes from the stability tech and structured testing. We barely noticed the difference, especially once we got moving.

Read More: Best Brooks Shoes for Walking.

Diana Rogers, DPM, a podiatric foot and ankle surgery specialist in Crystal Lake, Illinois, and Casey Pidich, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon based in the Bronx, Newly introduced York, both recommend Hoka’s Clifton series to patients for arch support, so you know it's a good one.

According to recent reports, pidich loves that the design encourages great form—the sole ensures that your feet rock off the ground rather than push off your toes. Rogers specifically recommends the shoe for her plantar fasciitis (a condition where you feel pain in the arch) patients for this exact reason. “The lightweight feel on this shoe propels feet forward rather than making them do extra work,” she says.

WH style editor Shannon Zitz found in her testing that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. “My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe,” she noted, noting that her stride felt smooth and natural.

The Clifton 11 is available in wide and extra-wide sizing, making it a good fit for a wide variety of walkers.

In a recent development, read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro.

Sources indicate that for those who appreciate a good slip-on shoe, the Skechers Go Walk Flex Azriel’s lightweight, breathable mesh upper is great for sweaty feet, while hovering around a bargain price of about $60 (and on sale for cheaper sometimes). The ultra-cushioned midsole offers great arch support, too.

“This is a solid no-frills walking shoe that’s perfect for errands, quick hot girl strolls, or for walking your dog,” says WH style editor Shannen Zitz. “I love that it slips on easily while still having the appearance of a classic sneaker with bungee laces that never come undone.”.

Zitz was skeptical about whether the slip-on would be supportive and secure enough, but the breathable, stretchy mesh offered surprisingly good compression around her feet.

In a recent development, “It keeps my feet locked in and has never caused any pain or blisters,” she claims. “While I wouldn’t log miles in this shoe, it is cushioned and supportive enough for long periods of standing or casual wear.” However, she finds the style a bit orthopedic-looking, although the white colorway can look cute with jeans or dresses.

Read More: Best Skechers For Walking.

In a recent development, asics is considered a classic, all-around great brand for walking, especially if you struggle with overpronation (ankles that roll inward) or have flat feet. Take the Gel-Kayano 32, which has thick foam borders on each side to encourage proper alignment and walking gait. Deep heel cups also help keep arches supported—there’s a reason this shoe made our best plantar fasciitis walking shoe guide.

Industry observers note that fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi is a huge fan of the firm, stiffer midsole that still maintains massive plushness with its signature gel cushioning system for superior shock absorption. “My landings feel like I’m hovering above ground, which states a lot given I stomp on hard pavement daily. I actually find it more cushioned than the Hoka Mach 6,” she says. The heel-to-toe drop is 8 millimeters, which Accardi says is a bit high for her liking, but ideal if you want to take all the pressure away from your arches.

The Hoka Mach 7 is Zitz’s personal favorite. While it’s technically a running shoe, she loves it for recovery and walking. “I’ve been living in this sneaker since returning from a week-long hiking trip where I logged about 20K steps per day,” she says. “It’s flexible, lightweight, and cushioned—it basically feels like a hug for my super tired feet.” The cushioning also doesn’t feel bulky compared to other Hoka models, such as the Bondi 8.

The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. Zitz tested this shoe after it first dropped, walking more than 150 miles in it—and not once did she feel even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

Another brownie point? It comes in wide sizing. Some WH editors find standard Hoka sizing pretty narrow, but the wide fit has adequate space in the toe box, so you can walk for hours without experiencing any friction. For extra room overall, podiatrist Shital Sharma, DPM, a podiatrist at Pinewood Family Care Co. in New Jersey, recommends going up a half-size in all walking sneakers because your feet tend to swell and expand from physical activity.

In a recent development, lined with mesh to make this an ultra-breathable sneaker, the Pegasus is a winner because it has a slim, low heel that Perkins notes is awesome for maintaining a smooth walking cadence. We love that the 42 is lighter than the previous model and has a curvier toe box that gives more toe spring, a smoother ride, and a roomier fit.

WH Fitness Director Jacqueline Andriakos has worn countless versions of the Nike Pegasus for both running and walking and has logged hundreds of miles in it. “I find the sole a bit on the firmer side, and the mesh upper really hugs and forms to your individual foot shape,” she says. “The shoe feels perfectly snug and secure as you step without being too constricting.”.

Recent findings suggest that she does flag that the tongue sometimes gets folded up and tucked under the laces in a slightly uncomfortable way. “I fix this by being really diligent when I put the shoes on, making sure to pull the tongue taut and make sure it's lying flat before tying my shoes.”.

The shoe is super breathable and lightweight, which makes it a great option for spring and summer, but less so for cold or wet weather. Overall, this is Andriakos’ go-to walking shoe recommendation for her friends and family—and so far she's only heard happy feedback from loved ones who have purchased a Pegasus shoe.

The latest edition of the Fresh Foam X 1080 wows us with its inclusive sizing, with narrow, standard, wide, and extra-wide fits available to accommodate all feet.

It has been revealed that “I have a hard time finding walking shoes that are both cushioned and supportive enough for my high arches and sensitive balls of the feet, but that are also narrow enough,” Andriakos claims. “This is absolutely perfect if you deal with any foot pain concerns or struggle with sneakers being a bit too wide—I have walked over 100 miles in these at this point and have never even had a sore or tender spot from rubbing or chafing (they also required zero break-in period).”Andriakos also finds the laces are very secure and don’t come untied easily. The only downside? “When I’ve worn it on rainy days, I notice my feet will feel damp and it takes a bit to dry out.” To help combat that, she just throws it in the dryer (which, to be clear, isn’t recommended by the brand, but she found it hasn't damaged the silhouette!).

Read More: Best Fresh Balance Shoes.

Sources indicate that the On Cloudtilt Remix is built for walking, thanks to its sequence of collapsing “cloud” foam to deliver a smooth, plush ride. It has maximum cushioning and bounce, compared to lots of other walking shoes we’ve tested, making it a solid pick for walkers and casual runners who prefer a softer, cushier feel underfoot.

Zitz recently added this pair to her collection and appreciates how lightweight and springy it feels. “I feel like I have such a pep in my step when I wear it—which is basically all the time since it’s so stylish,” she claims. “I love the layers of see-through mesh on the upper, which looks super modern and clean. I’ve been wearing this shoe nonstop with capris, leggings, and athletic shorts.”.

This style features Helion Superfoam (a blend of firm and flexible foam components) that delivers bounce without a lot of bulk. It also has a moderate 7 mm heel-to-toe drop, meaning it distributes weight evenly throughout the lower body, making it a pretty good pick for most walkers. It’s the perfect shoe that combines all our must-have walking shoe features into one sleek kick.

Industry observers note that the Newly introduced Balance 608 V5 Trainer has over 38,000 reviews on Amazon, and for good reason. The brand integrated its signature ABZORB midsole (a blend of substantial foam cushioning with compression resistance), which is designed to lessen the blow on joints when walking.

In a recent development, the 608 has tons of shock absorption which makes it great for neutral to high arches. But since it lacks stability features, it’s not our top choice for flat feet. We do like that it comes in narrow, standard, and wide sizing.

Industry observers note that ideally, walking shoes will assist with your gait (your walking pattern) instead of just cushioning impact. Your shoe should also be somewhat stiff—the more it bends, the less stability it will have.

Sources indicate that to test the flexibility, hold the shoe at the toe box and heel counter and try to fold the shoe in half by pushing on its ends to see how sturdy it is. If it folds in half or twists with ease, it’s too flexible, says podiatrist Elizabeth Daughtry, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle specialist with Foot and Ankle Specialists of the Mid-Atlantic in Cary, North Carolina.

She also adds that seeking out a shoe with a boat-like (rockered) shape, rigid midsole, and firm heel counter can help stabilize feet, control overpronation (collapsing arches), and prevent heel striking.

Look for walking shoes that have an outsole with more rigidity in the midsole for stability. Different feet have different needs, so it’s important to have insoles that can be removed in case you use orthotics. “Most shoes don’t offer adequate support alone,” states Dr. Daughtry. “You should supplement most shoes with a more custom-molded orthotic, which your local podiatrist can make for you, as this provides adequate support and helps with shock absorption, while also allowing for additional cushioning.”.

In a recent development, testing footwear is something we’re a little obsessive about, and we’re testing walking shoes on a constant basis. Over the past year alone, we’ve tested over 100 walking shoes, paying attention to fit, comfort, support, and durability. To narrow it down even further, we also consulted podiatrists and certified trainers about their favorite picks.

Additional reporting by Nicolette Accardi.

RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F.
  • Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.
  • A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

It has been revealed that in December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” stated Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

Recent findings suggest that “The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse remarked. “There has been no fresh data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”.

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

It has been revealed that A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse stated.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”.

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse noted.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”.

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination initiative for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse remarked.

It has been revealed that “There have been no upcoming studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ upcoming patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

In a recent development, originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

Sources indicate that to be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow people to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

In a recent development, there are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Industry observers note that okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your massive-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

In a recent development, endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he remarked.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

In a recent development, stuparich remarked endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”.

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:.

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

Recent findings suggest that “These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel noted.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

It has been revealed that some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:.

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel stated. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

Latest Update: 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor.
  • In a recent development, we’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance.
  • It has been revealed that there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” claims global editorial director Amy Astley. “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!”.

In a recent development, we’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD-approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present.

It has been revealed that there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home. Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley indicates in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors.

According to recent reports, created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work.

Recent findings suggest that global features director Sam Cochran’s debut coffee table book opens with the words, “Nothing is interesting unless it is personal.” His project, American Designers at Home, brings that idea to life beautifully. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—claims, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur.

Levasseur indicates that Simon Upton’s most recent release with Rizzoli contains “beauty and poetry on every page.” The title is a nod to the iconic London A–Z: The detailed street atlas that every Londoner seemed to own in the 1980s and early 2000s, pre-Google Maps. Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.”.

Recent findings suggest that this beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” says senior digital editor Catherine Hong. “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration.".

Sources indicate that “Whether or not you’d ever dare to decorate with Sasha Bikoff’s over-the-top flair, this book is guaranteed to make a splash on your coffee table,” states Hong. Behind its trippy, hot-pink cover lies screaming color, clashing eras, and utter fantasy. The designer lives by her “Rule of Three Wows”—chronicled in the pages—and her book is, accordingly, loud, wildly fun, and a little bit insane in the best way.

It has been revealed that studio Valle de Valle’s debut monograph offers a refined window into the AD100 firm’s singular vision and creative evolution—surveying 10 projects from the past 10 years. Printed in Italy, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson, the pages demonstrate the firm’s interior philosophy of creating spaces that feel personal, layered, and deeply inhabitable. “The edition isn’t just a tour de visual force, it’s an art object unto itself,” indicates Cochran. “I would expect nothing less from these brilliant auteurs.".

“One of Meyer Davis’s greatest strengths is how cofounders Will Meyer and Gray Davis distill references, ideas, and desires into a highly refined vision,” notes AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach. As client Jenna Lyons puts it in the book’s foreword, “They gave me clarity.” Beyond a printed body of work, The Language of Home is a testament to the collaborations that shape the studio's warm, reductive interiors. Designed with honest materials and a contemporary lens, the featured residences—a modern glass house in the Berkshires and an earthen dwelling in Puerto Escondido—reflect their inhabitants with a calm, clear ease.

Sources indicate that the inaugural monograph from AD100 design duo Humbert & Poyet showcases their signature brand of eclectic French luxury, blending Art Deco glamour, midcentury modernism, and the decorative arts. Spanning residential and hospitality projects around the world, the book by AD contributing editor Gay Gassmann takes readers from a French Riviera villa to a Milan restaurant housed in a 17th-century chapel, with stops in Newly introduced York, Paris, Monaco, and Seoul.

In New York: Atelier AM, Alexandra and Michael Misczynkski, the married couple behind the AD100 firm, shine a light on their New York projects, all beautifully captured by François Halard. Spotlighting a range of projects like elegant Manhattan residences and more relaxed Long Island retreats, contributor Ingrid Abramovitch indicates the book itself is “equally exquisite, with a cover resembling wood grain, and high-gloss pages printed in Italy.”.

Recent findings suggest that 2026 AD Latest American Voices honoree Amber Guyton first burst onto the design scene by way of her hit blog, Blessed Little Bungalow. “Her debut book brings the same wit and spirit to the printed page in a kaleidoscope of color and pattern,” indicates Cochran. Senior shopping editor Nashia Baker adds that the pages “truly embody how to bring personality to any room.” Throughout the book, she makes a case for maximalism, and distills her approach into four pillars: joy, culture, layers, and intention.

Recent findings suggest that “This book is perfect for cinephiles, design-lovers, or anyone with a case of wanderlust,” claims senior digital editor Rachel Wallace. Film is one way to travel the world without ever leaving the sofa, and with her new project On Location, longtime AD contributor Cathy Whitlock takes readers on a global cinematic journey. The book goes behind the scenes of films that make you want to hop on a flight and never look back. Colorful Mexico City scenes from Frida and Marie Antoinette’s famous Palace of Versailles shooting location are both represented.

Recent findings suggest that organized by a series of chapter essays rather than specific projects, AD100 designer Dan Fink’s debut book explores bigger questions on how spaces, objects, and compositions move us across time. At the same time, the book spotlights several career-defining projects from his namesake studio, including previously unpublished interiors like Manhattan penthouses, Hawaiian beach retreats, Hollywood homes, and more.

Industry observers note that one of the few completely fail-proof gifts is one of the best coffee table books of the season—weighty tomes whose thick, glossy pages feature stunning photographs and illustrations, to be specific. On a superficial level, they add ambiance, whether you place them in a library or a living room. But the best ones live in your home forever, while expanding your horizons far beyond. They also come across as far more memorable and thoughtful than the expected candle or bottle of champagne. Like works of fiction, there are limitless topics that can make deciding on an eye-catching hardcover (that doubles as home decor) seemingly impossible.

But that’s where we come in. Our team has gathered its favorite giftable recommendations for everyone from tennis enthusiasts to globe-trotters to interior design aficionados. From a book focused on hotels around the world to another that spotlights Tokyo style, there are plenty of ways to adorn the coffee tables of all the people on your holiday gift list. Most of them came out in 2024, but we’ve also included a few evergreen picks that make worthy gifts any year.

Plus, if you’re down to the wire on last-minute gifts, rest assured that most of these selections are available (and even marked down ahead of the holidays!) on Amazon.

Après-ski style needs no introduction in a season full of fuzzy Fair Isle sweaters, but it’s the cozy interiors of the chalets along the world’s most popular ski slopes that are worthy of a second look. From the wooden beams of an A-frame to the blazing fireplaces set within them, AD contributor Kathryn O’Shea-Evans pores over the finer details in this fun, wintery escape.

As associate digital editor Maya Ibbitson previously described it, “Alpine Style is a true compendium of resort luxury,” spanning spectacular chalets from Gstaad to Aspen and featuring the works of AD PRO Directory members such as Massucco Warner, Robbins Architecture, and Kara Adam Interiors.

Japan’s interiors are a perpetual reference for modern-day designers, and whether you’re a proponent of wabi-sabi principles or just looking for small space ideas, Tokyo Style will help you explore both.

Originally published in 1993, it’s since become a collector’s item and cult classic, and it was recommended by commerce writer Julia Harrison for anyone who would appreciate a more intimate glimpse of Tokyo’s dwellings: “Apartamento, an imprint that consistently delivers on elite design, has reintroduced Tsuzuki’s collection for us to enjoy in its full brilliance—that is, not a ‘fine’ condition original at $170 with $90 shipping from eBay.”.

Prefaced with a foreword by Spike Lee, BLK MKT Vintage peers into the world of the Brooklyn antique shop’s endlessly curious founders Jannah Handy and Kiyanna Stewart. “This monograph teems with more than 300 studies of vintage ephemera and reads like a collage with context, or an I spy for your inner adult archivist,” writes Ibbitson of the book. For collectors, Sydney Gore pinpoints it as a must-have for your rotation.

Donald Judd’s considered, minimalist approach to design has fostered its own cult of acolytes who, these days, emulate his daybeds and chairs on Instagram.

According to recent reports, for the true Juddheads, the Judd Foundation has produced a upcoming book edited by his children Rainer and Flavin Judd that chronicles more than one hundred of his functional works produced between 1970 and 1992. “Mixed in are the juiciest bits: photos from past and present of those pieces in Judd-designed spaces in New York and Marfa,” Ibbitson writes.

AD’s Milan correspondent Laura May Todd penned a delightful homage to Italian living this year, one which spans from historic palaces in Venice to the homes of creatives like Luca Guadagnino along with midcentury Milanese apartments, so you can enjoy a small taste of la dolce vita on each page.

It was one of the AD PRO team’s favorite book releases this fall, one which should suit the person on your list who never got over their Italian study abroad or is manifesting a Sicilian villa in their future.

For the person on your list who delights in having people over, How They Entertain, released this fall, serves as a comprehensive guide to (and celebration of) the art of hosting.

Written by Pierre Sauvage, it’s chock-full of inspiration for your next dinner party, from recipes to design notes on arranging a tabletop to remember, as well as interviews with tastemakers like Laura Gonzalez about their particular philosophy on entertaining guests.

Considering this year’s smash summer hit Challengers and the enduring popularity of tenniscore (polos, skorts, and all), it’s clear that tennis is a lifestyle that has captured the imagination of many people, avid tennis players or not.

This book recommended by the AD PRO team earlier this year is dedicated to a more, uh, underserved cross section of the sport: the backdrops where athletes volley their way to tournament glory (clay, grass, asphalt, and beyond) in locales from Queens to Kenya.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent is no stranger to the pages of this very magazine, and his new book is a friends and family affair studded with stars, like Oprah and legendary choreographer Fatima Robinson, with whom Brent has formed close connections over the past 20 years.

We’ve previously described the book (layered with sentimental photos and upcoming snapshots of contributors in their home) as “more scrapbook than design manifesto, a love letter to the spaces that people have inhabited and inherited over the years.” Read AD’s extensive interview with Brent for more backstory behind (and tidbits from) the book.

For art buffs with a fondness for the Harlem Renaissance—an era synonymous with greats like Aaron Douglas, known as the father of African-American art—this new book compiled by MoMA curator Denise Murrell is an excellent title to know. “Having this book is about as close as you’ll ever get to owning one of the original masterpieces featured in the Harlem Renaissance exhibition at The Met,” Gore says.

Industry observers note that self-interested plug here, but we really couldn’t publish a guide to coffee table books without mentioning our own, AD at 100: A Century of Style. For the design buff with an appetite for lush interiors and a healthy curiosity for how A-listers live, there’s no more satisfying holiday treat than this tome that delves into the homes of the Obamas, David Hockney, Diana Vreeland, and beyond. It also serves as a bird’s eye view of a century in design and architecture, including the works of Frank Gehry, David Hicks, Frank Lloyd Wright, and much, much more.

Architecture has a reputation for myopia when it comes to its foremost voices, but this book seeks to rectify the past with a fresh overview of some of its most brilliant underrepresented talents, including interviews with female architects around the globe such as Tatiana Bilbao, Liz Diller, and Julia Gamolina.

“100 Women offers a refreshing reframe of the built environment outside of the male-dominated Western canon, proving the benefits of sourcing alternative points of reference,” Ibbitson wrote of it in AD PRO’s guide to the best newly introduced design books out this past spring.

Colony founder Jean Lin has mentored and platformed some of the design world’s brightest rising stars, and in her first book out this year, she tapped a wide pool of creatives to explore the concept of collections that inform their work, from ceramicist Stephanie H. Shih’s cache of soy sauce bottles to Mira Nakashima’s stockpile of lumber inherited from her father, architect turned furniture maker George Nakashima.

Recent findings suggest that that’s just one facet of the book Ibbitson previously described as an “encyclopedic, elemental study of artist studios, profiles, materials, and everything else under the design umbrella,” with plenty of wisdom imparted within its pages, from how-tos to styling tips. Read our interview with Lin for more of her notes on curating a collection of your own.

Luna Luna—a 1980s artist-led amusement park featuring works by icons of the art world such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Salvador Dalí, and David Hockney—is experiencing a resurgence as of late, what with a newly introduced retrospective at The Shed this year, along with a revival of the park itself in Los Angeles late last year.

Recent findings suggest that this 2023 book takes a deeper dive into Luna Luna’s history blending fine art with the playful energy of a carnival—encompassing rides, interactive installations, and surreal sculptures. It comes recommended by associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz, who nods to the book’s breadth of archival media within, from photos to sketches, that are accompanied by behind-the-scenes stories.

In a recent development, for jet-setters who love to live large on vacation, Spencer Bailey’s Design: The Leading Hotels of the World (released just this month) is one sure way to sustain a sense of wanderlust. His newly introduced book takes readers on a visual journey to 80 countries around the globe, inviting them to mentally book into sumptuous spaces from The Okura in Tokyo to the Portrait Hotel in Milan. It’s rounded out by notable travel and design writers like Maria Cristina Didero and Mark Ellwood, who lend us their travel tips, on top of their reflections on the lodgings featured within.

According to recent reports, as a society, we’re in our protein era, and that’s a good thing. The macronutrient is super key for building and repairing muscles, everyday body functionality, and immune and hormone health. Plus, it helps keep you full.

Recent findings suggest that since it's so important, it's also no surprise that you need quite a bit of it, even though pulling that off might get a little tricky sometimes. While the recommended dietary allowance for protein has remained the same for 30 years—at 0.36 grams per pound of total body weight, or 0.8 grams per kilogram—research now suggests that we need more like one gram per pound. (Psst: that higher number is especially important for anyone who regularly hits the gym.) One easy way to make sure you get there? Following high-protein recipes, where all the calculations are already done for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its newly introduced NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

It has been revealed that when the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The firm’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The upcoming NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

It has been revealed that on top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

It has been revealed that power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

It has been revealed that why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it.

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the latest NX7 in the comments, today.
