💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it only makes sense to want to give your weight loss journey everything you’ve got.
  • In a recent development, here's the truth: The average person cannot safely lose 10 pounds in a month, says Michael Glickman, MD, a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness.
  • It has been revealed that meet the experts: Michael Glickman, MD, is a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it only makes sense to want to give your weight loss journey everything you’ve got. And, if you’re into big goals, you may wonder if it’s safe to lose 10 pounds in a month.

In a recent development, here's the truth: The average person cannot safely lose 10 pounds in a month, says Michael Glickman, MD, a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness. Losing weight at this aggressive of a pace can raise your risk of developing gallstones (painful deposits of digestive fluid in the gallbladder) and up the odds that you’ll regain the weight down the line, he says. (Neither of those are ideal!).

It has been revealed that meet the experts: Michael Glickman, MD, is a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness. Michael Hamlin, CSCS, is a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness.

Of course, everyone is different and a lot depends on your starting weight. Also, you can still have aggressive goals when it comes to weight loss—it’s just that 10 pounds in a too-short timeframe is a tricky benchmark for most people. So, how much weight can you safely lose in a month—and how should you even go about it? Here’s what experts suggest.

According to recent reports, the timeline will be different for everyone, given factors like starting weight, genetics, nutrition, activity level, stress, and more. But Dr. Glickman says to give yourself anywhere from two to three months to hit that 10-pounds-lost goal. “For some, this could take longer, so be compassionate with your body and prioritize what’s best for your health,” he says.

When it comes to how much weight is safe to lose at a given time, stick to one to two pounds per week, states Dr. Glickman. “Some people can shed weight more quickly in the first month after instituting a lower calorie and healthy diet, however much of the weight loss on the scale will have been due to water weight.”.

If you have obesity and are revamping your eating habits, along with starting an exercise program after being fairly sedentary, you may see bigger gains early on than someone with a lower starting weight who isn’t making drastic changes.

First things first: A safe way to lose weight is a holistic and multi-factorial approach that involves optimal nutrition, frequent exercise, stress reduction, and adequate sleep, notes Dr. Glickman. It's not necessarily about eating less but being conscious of the diversity of plants in your diet, and the avoidance of processed foods, refined oils, and refined carbohydrates, he explains.

On top of that, apply sustainable healthy changes to your routine that you enjoy, notes Michael Hamlin, CSCS, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness. Maybe that means attending a workout class with friends twice a week, cooking a plant-based dinner with your partner, or throwing on your favorite podcast and going for a solo walk.

According to recent reports, sleep deprivation promotes an increase in ghrelin, your hunger hormone, which can trigger late night snacking, ultimately increasing your daily caloric intake, says Dr. Glickman. So do your best to get seven to nine hours of sleep per night. Not only that, getting more sleep helps you feel more energized, so you can add more activity to your day.

According to recent reports, it may sound simple, but 30 minutes of daily walking can do wonders, says Dr. Glickman. “It isn’t about calorie burning—it’s about the mobility, the happy hormones your brain releases, and the physiological anti-inflammatory responses that have long-term impacts on your weight.”.

Getting daily steps in has health benefits ranging from lowering your risk of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease to helping you live longer. While any movement is good, moving at a brisk pace is the best way to get in all those extra perks.

Plant diversity has been shown to have the most beneficial impact on the gut microbiome, which influences your metabolic set point (the body’s preferred weight), insulin levels, and fat storage, notes Dr. Glickman. Plant-based diets are also linked to a lower risk of developing heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, making this a big win for your overall health, too.

Industry observers note that his suggestion? Try a plant-based day or meal per week to ensure you’re supporting your gut microbiome and loading up on the veggies.

It has been revealed that it’s best to consult a doctor or registered dietitian to determine your daily caloric needs since it depends on your age, gender, activity level, muscle mass, current weight, and the amount of calories you burn at rest (a.k.a. your basal metabolic rate), says Hamlin. From there, they can determine a slight calorie deficit, or how many calories you need in a day to lose one to two pounds a week, he explains.

Industry observers note that while you’re waiting for a consult, check out the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases’ online body weight planner. It asks you to enter some basic information like your current weight, your ideal weight, and your activity level, and provides what your daily calorie goals should be to help you get there.

“Stress can lead to increased hunger hormones and an elevated metabolic set point,” states Dr. Glickman. Higher levels of the stress hormone cortisol can create stubborn fat distribution around the abdomen, he adds.

Sources indicate that although this one is often easier said than done, to help combat stress and anxiety, try relaxation techniques like meditation, yoga, and journaling. And, of course, if you’re struggling with stress management, consider reaching out to a mental health therapist for individual guidance on navigating everything.

“Sometimes we can mistake the feeling of thirst for hunger, so make sure to stay hydrated throughout the day, especially during and after exercise,” Dr. Glickman says. Women should drink about 11.5 cups (2.7 liters) of fluids a day, per Mayo Clinic. (Note: That total can come from food and liquids.).

Industry observers note that strength training has a significant impact on your metabolism and fat burning capabilities, studies show, so incorporate resistance training at least three days a week, claims Dr. Glickman. Just take note that because strength training builds muscle, you may notice little or even no overall weight change at times, even though you are losing fat. (Not sure where to start with your strength training journey? Try Women's Health's The Woman's Guide To Strength Training: Dumbbells.).

In a recent development, HIIT workouts burn a ton of calories and can change your body composition while building muscle, says Hamlin. In fact, women who incorporated HIIT programming achieved similar body composition and aerobic capacity results in half the time as women who did moderate-intensity workouts, a 2017 study published in the Journal of Diabetes Research found.

Fiber helps regulate blood sugar levels, prevent insulin resistance and diabetes, and is an excellent source of nutrition for healthy bacteria in the gut, states Dr. Glickman. High-fiber foods like vegetables are also filling without overloading on the calories, explains Hamlin. You can get fiber in powder or supplement form, but your best (and healthiest) bet is from plants, adds Dr. Glickman.

Weight gain is linked with the consumption of highly processed and packaged foods, Dr. Glickman says. “This includes any food item in a wrapper with ingredients you can’t pronounce, even if the calories and carbohydrates seem appealing,” he explains. “Always choose whole foods over packaged ones.”.

Sources indicate that do your best to prioritize cooking at home to eliminate sneaky fats, sugars, and processed ingredients that are not listed on a menu, claims Dr. Glickman.

In a recent development, focus on the quality of food on your plate and aim for three hearty meals a day that include a small amount of complex carbohydrates (root veggies and whole grains), a moderate amount of high-quality protein (fish, chicken, eggs, and tofu), and lots of plant-based fiber, says Dr. Glickman.

Alcoholic drinks lack nutritional value and are usually packed with calories, so it’s best to scale back on booze, indicates Hamlin. When you drink alcohol, it also immediately goes to the liver where it’s prioritized as an energy source, so your body burns alcohol cals first. Not only that, alcohol also lowers your inhibitions and raises the odds you’ll eat more than you need to feel satiated.

Industry observers note that to help with accountability, Hamlin suggests using a food journal or app to track your meals. This will give you a better understanding and awareness of how many calories you’re consuming and at which meal. Research shows this is an effective way to lose weight, too. One study found that people who tracked their meals at least five days of each week had “significant and sustained weight loss” over time compared to people who tracked less or inconsistently.

Industry observers note that it can take time for your stomach to recognize when it’s full, so pause in between portions before deciding if you actually want more, says Hamlin. You can either pre-pack your meals with smaller portion sizes or use smaller plates to provide a visual cue. One scientific analysis of 14 studies found that people who ate smaller portions had a “substantial” drop in how many calories they ate each day.

Sources indicate that think long-term about weight loss and establish a goal that is realistic for your lifestyle, says Hamlin. Your goals might take time and patience, but that’s okay, he adds. “Weight loss isn't solely about a caloric deficit, because the body is a super complex piece of machinery, and we can't simply boil all of weight loss down to calories in versus calories out.”.

  • It has been revealed that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • In a recent development, just before 4 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators states Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

It has been revealed that police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

In a recent development, just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

According to recent reports, jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

According to recent reports, then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report states the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

It has been revealed that A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson stated the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody stated a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and claims it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

Sources indicate that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

Sources indicate that A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

Recent findings suggest that in 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

In a recent development, the NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

Sources indicate that september may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Recent findings suggest that three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

Sources indicate that that's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Recent findings suggest that compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

It has been revealed that tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

It has been revealed that either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

It has been revealed that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon. In the case of fine wool shawls from Kashmir—prized among 19th-century Europeans, including Joséphine Bonaparte—the word cashmere stuck. For Kadri Mujtaba, a fascination with these textiles came early. Born into a family of merchants and weavers in the region’s city of Srinagar, he observed a deep-rooted culture around hand-spun yarn and small wooden looms.

A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.

One of the studio’s handmade shawl looms.

A Doorway Sozni twill blanket draped over a chair.

“It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he says of the technique, passed down for centuries. Amid encroaching mechanization, Mujtaba has stayed committed to slow craft, cultivating a network of some 2,000 artisans over the past two decades. Initially he’d create custom pieces for designers and brands (Pierre Yovanovitch, The Row, Luis Laplace) and host high-end trunk shows. That is how Jonathan Renker—via his father, a longtime customer—first encountered the wares. Now, he and Mujtaba have partnered on Kadri: a new brand of cashmere accessories and home goods that marry Kashmiri refinement and streamlined design.

A Jaali Kaani blanket on the grounds of Pari Mahal garden.

A wood swift of cashmere yarn at the Kadri atelier.

Shawls and scarves from Kadri’s debut collection.

Recent findings suggest that the company debuts with a collection of scarves, throws, and blankets. The cofounders enlisted creative director Dan Thawley and textile designer Maeva Elfassi, who distilled the Kashmir Valley landscape into shades of tobacco, lime, vermilion, and—as a nod to Srinagar’s Dal Lake—dusty blue. Wool from Changthangi goats, which graze across the plateaus of nearby Ladakh, is spun by hand, resulting in airy, ultrasoft knits. More impressive still is the subtlety on display. A bouclé piece has the immersive pull of a Color Field painting, while a quilted scarf joins two paper-thin layers. Just one blanket requires months of work and a balletic dance of bobbins.

Recent findings suggest that “What makes Kadri so special is this research-and-development approach,” claims Renker, describing a push toward novel applications while holding fast to the handmade vernacular. “The only electricity that’s used are the overhead lights on a cloudy day.”.

Recent findings suggest that late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Sources indicate that charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

We’ve got stretchy trousers that look pretty darn good, a solid pair of sneakers, and layers that work alone or together. It's about finding clothes that do a little bit of everything, especially if you like to travel light.

If you’re looking to spruce up your fit for your next flight (and to become someone’s airport crush), here’s what to know.

I'm not saying you can't wear jeans on a plane, but why would you when you have so many more comfortable alternatives? You'll be sitting for hours, probably in a seat that doesn't give you much room to move, so the last thing you want is a waistband digging into your stomach. Look for pants with a little stretch, breathable fabrics, and a relaxed fit that won't feel restrictive when you're sitting down. Brands like Vuori and DUER have gotten particularly good at making pants that feel like loungewear without necessarily looking like it. And if you're committed to sweatpants, that's perfectly fine, too. Just go for a pair with a cleaner, more structured fit.

Reigning Champ Midweight Terry Relaxed Sweatpant.

Nike Club Open Hem Brushed Fleece Pants.

You really don't need to overthink your airport T-shirt. A good cotton tee will do just fine, especially if it's something you already wear regularly. Personally, I'd avoid anything too tight or made from a heavy fabric, since airports and airplanes can get surprisingly stuffy. A slightly relaxed fit gives you more room to move and makes layering easier, too. I tend to gravitate toward simple, solid-colored tees because they go with practically anything. Uniqlo's AIRism Cotton Oversized T-Shirt is a good example of something that's affordable, comfortable, and easy to dress up or down depending on what else you're wearing.

Mack Weldon Pima Long Sleeve T-Shirt.

Everlane The Essential Organic Crew.

Recent findings suggest that I don't care if you're flying to Miami in the middle of July; bring a sweatshirt. Airplane cabins have a habit of feeling like refrigerators, and I'd much rather have an extra layer than spend an entire flight shivering. A good crewneck or hoodie is probably all you need, preferably something soft that isn't too bulky to stuff into your bag when you're not wearing it. I'm partial to oversized sweatshirts for traveling, though you don't need to go so significant that you're drowning in fabric. Something like Alo's Accolade Crewneck works well because you can wear it with sweatpants or a nicer pair of trousers. And honestly, if you're desperate, a sweatshirt can always double as a makeshift pillow.

Abercrombie SwEssential Popover 2.0 Hoodie.

Todd Snyder Champion Relaxed French Terry Crewneck.

Eddie Bauer Micro Polar Fleece Lined Pullover Hoodie.

Industry observers note that depending on where you're headed, a lightweight jacket might be one of the more useful things you bring. I'm not talking about a huge puffer or anything that'll take up half your carry-on. Think windbreakers, chore jackets, and lightweight layers that you can easily throw over a T-shirt or sweatshirt. If you're traveling somewhere with unpredictable weather, a technical jacket from Patagonia or Arc'teryx makes sense. Otherwise, a simple chore jacket from somewhere like Quince or Gap can make an otherwise basic airport outfit look a little more put-together. Plus, you'll probably wear it during the trip anyway, so it's one less thing to pack.

Quince 100% Organic Herringbone Twill Shirt Jacket.

Arc’teryx Atom Insulated Jacket.

It has been revealed that between getting to the airport, navigating security, and walking what feels like three miles to your gate, you'll probably spend more time on your feet than you realize. That's why I'd prioritize comfortable sneakers over anything else when putting together an airport outfit. You want a pair with good cushioning, enough support, and ideally something easy to slip on and off. Newly introduced Balance, Hoka, and On all make sneakers that fit the bill, though I'd stick with a pair you've already broken in rather than trying something new on travel day. And since you're probably only bringing one or two pairs of shoes on your trip, bonus points if they match the rest of your wardrobe.

On The Roger Centre Tennis Court Shoe.

It has been revealed that you really don't need much here. In fact, I'd argue the best airport outfits are pretty simple. But a few accessories can make even a basic T-shirt-and-sweatpants combination feel more intentional. A classic Yankees cap from '47 is great for early flights when you don't feel like doing your hair, and a good pair of sunglasses is always useful when you're heading somewhere sunny. I also like wearing a watch when I travel, mostly because I don't want to keep pulling out my phone to check the time. None of these things are essential, obviously, but they're easy ways to make the outfit feel a little more like your own.

Tifosi Veloce Sports Sunglasses.

Seiko Analog Green Dial Automatic Silver Stainless Steel Watch.

Hyundai IONIQ 5 caught with a new high-tech interior and major display screen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai appears to be testing a latest high-tech setup in the IONIQ 5.
  • Is the IONIQ 5 next in line for an overhaul?
  • Hyundai is betting heavily on software, AI, autonomous driving, robotics, and more as it expands from a traditional auto manufacturer to a “software-centric mobility leader.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai appears to be testing a latest high-tech setup in the IONIQ 5. A prototype was spotted with the door wide open, exposing a large display and a layout that looks very different from the current model.

Is the IONIQ 5 next in line for an overhaul? Another mysterious IONIQ 5 test mule was recently caught in a parking garage in South Korea, revealing what’s rumored to be Hyundai’s software-defined vehicle (SDV).

Hyundai is betting heavily on software, AI, autonomous driving, robotics, and more as it expands from a traditional auto manufacturer to a “software-centric mobility leader.”.

At the heart of it all is Hyundai Motor Group’s new Pleos Connect, an advanced in-vehicle infotainment and software platform.

Built on Android Automotive OS, Hyundai’s upcoming setup features a larger, tablet-style infotainment screen with apps, split-screen views, and more. It’s similar to using a smartphone with an easier-to-use, customizable layout.

The Grandeur was the first to launch with Hyundai’s Pleos in Korea in May, followed by the IONIQ 3 in Europe. In the US, the upcoming Tucson will be the first to go on sale with Pleos in early 2027.

Is the IONIQ 5 next in line? Hyundai aims to launch its first SDV as early as next year, and the IONIQ 5 appears to be a contender.

An IONIQ 5 test car was captured again (shown below) by @JHS_spyshot_official in a Korean parking garage, but this time the door was wide open, offering a clear view of the new setup.

A post shared by JHS (@jhs_spyshot_official).

Hyundai appeared to be testing automated parking features, and as you can see, the setup is considerably different from the current IONIQ 5.

According to recent reports, A large infotainment display sits at the center that appears to be running Hyundai Pleos, instead of the current dual 12.3″ screens. Meanwhile, the steering wheel and dash both appear to be completely redesigned.

Although it’s hard to see, previous spy images show the IONIQ 5 SDV test car with no driver display, with all information expected to move to the large center infotainment screen.

By 2030, Hyundai Motor Group intends to equip around 20 million Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis vehicles with the new Pleos setup.

Recent findings suggest that guess I'm holding onto my 2023 EV6 for as long as I can. I saw a preview of the new software and think it looks pretty solid, but I am NOT a fan of the "huge tablet" dashboard.

Industry observers note that my dad has a new Solterra and we took a long road trip in my EV6 last month. He mentioned my screens are so much more easy to see and use. The only matter I have is the top of the steering wheel obscures the icons at the top of my driver's screen, but I'd rather have that than a giant hulking tablet sitting in the middle of the dash.

The system is the “first tangible step” toward an SDV (Software-Defined Vehicle) architecture, Hyundai stated, which will unlock new in-car features, autonomous driving capabilities, and personalized driving experiences.

Over the summer, an IONIQ 6 prototype was spotted near Hyundai’s R&D hub in Europe with a similar high-tech setup.

With Hyundai planning to launch its first SDV as early as next year, we should learn more soon.

76 AD-Approved Interior Photographers in the Northeast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You name it, these interior photographers in the Northeast have shot it, in daylight and darkness, maximizing views of the park or the coast, the backyard or the city street far below.
  • Recent findings suggest that classical proportions and carefully composed details give William Abranowicz’s interior photos the poise of a still life.
  • This vibrant San Francisco home designed by Noz Nozawa is sometimes called “the Rainbow House.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand staircases. Cozy breakfast nooks. Color-drenched walls. You name it, these interior photographers in the Northeast have shot it, in daylight and darkness, maximizing views of the park or the coast, the backyard or the city street far below. Their images are portraits of homes, capturing a space’s personality and highlighting the talents of its designer. Read on to meet AD-approved interior photographers in the Northeast (and, in many cases, beyond).

A beachfront home in Santa Barbara, California.

Recent findings suggest that classical proportions and carefully composed details give William Abranowicz’s interior photos the poise of a still life. His background as a fine art printer shows in images that reward looking beyond the statement furniture to the smaller objects around it.

This vibrant San Francisco home designed by Noz Nozawa is sometimes called “the Rainbow House.”.

Sources indicate that brittany Ambridge makes colorful rooms shine and white rooms look luminous without losing the details that give them dimension. Her lighting approach draws on techniques learned shooting film, translating a home’s atmosphere whether the mood is airy and expansive, or bold and colorful. She has worked with talents including Jeremiah Brent, Nate Berkus, Charlotte Moss, and Gachot Studios.

Find your next creative collaborator using the AD PRO Sourcebook. Start exploring top interior photographers, stylists, decorative painters, millworkers, and more now.

The living room of Kate Upton and Justin Verlander’s penthouse in Latest York.

According to recent reports, dramatic natural lighting is often heightened and accentuated in Gieves Anderson’s photographs, in both moody, highly patterned rooms as well as light and airy spaces. He knows just how to make the most of a perfectly cast shadow.

An interior at the Maison Brummell Majorelle in Marrakech, Morocco.

Recent findings suggest that trained in classical and modern dance, Upcoming York City–based Emily Andrews parlays that craft’s contrasting principles of line and weight, positive and negative space, into her photography work. The beautifully captured balancing acts have garnered the attention of AD, WSJ Magazine, The New York Times, and others.

Glassworks offers a kaleidoscopic moment in a moody dining room.

If you love the enviable homes of Athena Calderone—a.k.a. EyeSwoon—Jessica Antola is a name you need to know. Antola has captured Calderone’s Instagram-famous spaces, as well as countless others.

The minimalist Brooklyn apartment of Coco Romack and Mars Hobrecker.

Winnie Au’s photography brings out the color and personality in each space she so smartly captures, whether it’s a playful Palm Springs hotel, a boldly designed Upcoming York apartment, or the creative studios of artists and makers.

A dining room in Greenwich, Connecticut, designed by Alison Hammatt Home.

Industry observers note that from Nantucket antiques to contemporary interiors, Jane Beiles approaches a room as a still life, balancing textures, shapes, and scale rather than letting one trophy piece steal the show. Based in Fairfield, Connecticut, she has photographed work by Gil Schafer, Katie Ridder, Stonefox, and Bennett Leifer.

Chloe Fineman’s West Village home, designed by Tali Roth.

Industry observers note that andrew Bui loves dynamic, expressive lighting and strives to create images with a timeless quality to them. He comes from two generations of award-winning restaurateurs, and his food photography is just as delectable as his interior shots.

Filmmaker ShawnLevy’s dining room in Manhattan, designed by AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent.

Industry observers note that raised in Texas and now based in Brooklyn, Max Burkhalter doesn’t shy away from assignments in the Lone Star State, having shot projects like David Adjaye’s crystalline Ruby City contemporary art center. Still, Burkhalter reps hard for Brooklyn and has collaborated with brands including In Common With and Roll & Hill.

Inside a 19th-century Brooklyn town house renovated by Hatchet Design & Build.

Sources indicate that nicholas Calcott has worked on a variety of editorial, commercial, and self-assigned projects across topics including home and belonging, creativity, and the future. He’s of Arabic, Jewish, and British heritage and also speaks French, so he brings an international sensibility to assignments.

The daughter of an architect and a photographer, Anita Calero brings an artistic eye to her still-life photography, and is equally adept at shooting nature and interiors. A celebrated fine-art photographer as well, Calero works between home bases in New York, Colombia, and Miami, living her philosophy that beauty is everywhere and “nothing is ugly.”.

Photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment in Brooklyn Heights.

A regular contributor to AD, Fresh York, and other publications, Seth Caplan documents spaces with a keen sense of presence, emphasizing warm tones and moody shadows. He loves a good portrait and also shoots images for homeware brands including Bed Threads, Framebridge, and Caraway Home.

Sean Davidson beautifully captures the stillness of an organically neutral interior.

A favorite of many AD100 and AD PRO Directory studios, Sean Davidson has translated his industrial design background into a successful career in photography, frequently working with top fashion brands and design publications alike.

A family home on Shelter Island.

Polished yet raw, Blaine Davis’s style and compositions result in interior shots and portraits that are crisp and authentic—not unlike the glossy pages of the magazines in which they appear. (Including AD, of course.).

A historic Fifth Avenue mansion, built by Stanford White.

According to recent reports, A documentary background shapes Hayley Ellen Day’s interest in the relationship between people and their spaces. Her interiors range from ornate salons to playful bathrooms, with small details offering clues to the lives unfolding beyond the frame.

Inside a reimagined 19th-century farmhouse in Southampton, Upcoming York, designer Ariel Okin animates a historic New York refuge using color and character.

Recent findings suggest that donna Dotan’s obsession with clean lines and natural light is evident across her catalog of interior shoots, in which spaces are portrayed as sun-kissed and in dazzling color. Her work has graced the pages of all major design publications, including AD.

A Latest York City apartment for Casameu New York, styled by Rebecca Bartoshesky.

Combining strong compositional elements with a sense of warmth and sensitivity, Pippa Drummond—a Kiwi photographer now based in Upcoming York City—has been commissioned by the likes of Dwell and Herman Miller.

Bovina Farm and Fermentory in Latest York’s Catskill Mountains.

It has been revealed that soft daylight and tactile finishes lend Sarah Elliott’s interiors an easy, unhurried feeling. Her photographs for Upstate invite a closer look at country living, while her work with Elizabeth Roberts, Nune, and others brings that intimacy to many homes.

A bedroom on the Upper East Side of Fresh York, designed by The Interiors Concierge and styled by Pablo Olguin.

It has been revealed that whether a space is minimalist or maximalist, Claire Esparros is able to distill its essence by amplifying the serenity or vibrancy of her photos. Framing spatial sequences and highlighting vignettes are among her strengths.

A landing in Kacey Musgraves’s Nashville home.

Lelanie Foster’s portraits of Serena Williams, Kacey Musgraves, and Misty Copeland for AD make the home as compelling as the person. For designers seeking photographs that introduce the inhabitants as well as the interiors, her portfolio merits a look.

A bedroom designed by Mieke ten Have and photographed by Frank Frances in Upcoming York’s Hudson Valley.

Trained in art practice at the School of Visual Arts, photographer Frank Frances has contributed his versatile eye to AD, British Vogue, West Elm, and others. His photography, which expands beyond interiors into beauty, food, and fashion, has appeared in exhibitions at galleries across the world, including Sasha Wolf Gallery, the Studio Museum of Harlem, and Werkstadt Graz.

Kirsten Francis captures a collectors’ trove.

According to recent reports, an NYC–based lifestyle photographer specializing in interiors and portraits, Kirsten Francis has shot sun-drenched spaces by a roster of designers including Ashley Darryl, Alyssa Kapito, and Emily C. Butler.

A family room in Park City, Utah, designed by Wendy Labrum Interiors.

Industry observers note that if Athena Calderone’s coffee table book Live Beautiful has earned a permanent spot on your coffee table, you’re already acquainted with Nicole Franzen’s photography. The Latest York talent’s portfolio also spans hospitality and cookbooks, giving homebodies and hosts alike something to savor.

Inside a private home on the Amalfi Coast.

The skill with which Patrick Fraser is able to portray history and character in his images is captivating. Born in the UK and recently relocated to Connecticut from the West Coast, he often takes inspiration from objects, landscapes, and people that have been forgotten or ignored.

In a recent development, every problem, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching.

The photographer shot his own kitchen on Long Island.

Douglas Friedman gives elaborate interiors a sense of drama, using natural light to bring out their materials. Along with photographing sumptuous rooms by Ken Fulk, Nicole Hollis, and Kelly Wearstler, the photographer has welcomed AD into his own Marfa retreat.

A modern retreat nestled in nature.

Sources indicate that alice Gao’s lens has been known to linger in shadows, resulting in a photograph that can romanticize even the most neutral, pared-back interiors. Her style brings minimalist, modern settings—such as those of clients Yabu Pushelberg and Toast UK, among others—beautifully to life.

This Brooklyn-based creative has brought an expert eye to shoots in countless stylish homes, restaurants like Altro Paradiso, and the studios of talents like Trueing and Christian Siriano.

The sunlit living room of a townhouse in Upcoming York City’s West Village.

His training as a painter informs Gaut’s portrait-like images of interiors, imbuing each space with personality. AD has published his images of Latest York apartments, ski chalets in Wyoming, and farmhouses in Nova Scotia, but he’s also a fine art photographer whose prints have appeared in stores including Design Within Reach.

Inside celeb stylist Kate Young’s upstate New York home.

In a recent development, family life in all its facets is a frequent muse for William Geddes—his own wife and daughters included—though he’s also keen on assignments across the editorial, advertising, and publishing industries. A graduate of The Newly introduced School, Parsons School for Design, Geddes also offers both simple and complex video shoots among his professional services.

A vignette from Elsa Perretti’s home in Spain.

Adrianna Glaviano finds visual wit in the smallest arrangements, such as jewelry on striped straws, or personal effects gathered around a sink. Her still-life sensibility offers designers a way to make the objects within a room part of its story. Working between New York and Milan, she counts AD France, HAY, FLOS, and Gohar World among her clients.

An Upstate Upcoming York couple painstakingly restored this geometric 1970s hideaway.

Golden hour appears to be Nick Glimenakis’s choice time to shoot, when he’s able to capture the warm light, long shadows, and exaggerated contrasts that up the drama in his imagery.

An indoor-outdoor space designed by Mike Moser Studio.

Residential design and hospitality meet in Christian Harder’s portfolio, which includes work with Jake Arnold, Ash, and AvroKO. His photographs of Darren Jett’s Brooklyn apartment for AD offer a useful introduction to his eye for rooms with personality. He’s also kept up a fine art photography practice and is repped by OneWay Gallery in Providence and Narragansett, Rhode Island.

In a Malibu home designed by Lala Reimagined, a dining area is filled with bentwood and natural fiber delights.

Ori Harpaz’s sharp editorial style has landed him multiple features in all of the top design magazines. His eye for color and penchant for strict angles mean his images are bold, striking, and arresting.

A marble bathroom in a Finger Lakes estate designed by Jeremiah Brent.

Ethan Herrington’s career began in commercial still-life photography, and places and things get equal billing in his portfolio—welcome news for those who obsess over both the room and its contents. Based in Cold Spring, New York, he has worked with Billy Cotton, Commune, and Studio Dorion.

A sunken living room oozes cool in this airy abode.

Formerly a fashion and textile print designer, Angela Hau—who operates out of San Francisco and NYC—has adapted her keen understanding of shape, scale, and balance to photography. Industry brands Thompson Street Studio, Egg Collective, and more have tapped Hau to beautifully capture interiors and product photography.

Studio Valle de Valle transformed a historic home in Toronto.

Jenni Kayne’s Los Angeles home and Neal Beckstedt’s wood-clad Chelsea apartment have both met Stephen Kent Johnson’s lens. He favors intimate views and revealing details over an all-encompassing wide angle, complete with soft light and carefully framed vignettes.

Inside a renovated California cabin with interiors designed by Fritz Haeg and Jeremy Schipper.

Industry observers note that recently relocated from LA, André Jones brings a sunny and warm approach to architecture and lifestyle photography. From rustic home interiors to sleek corporate buildings, his images are consistently well-framed and proportioned.

The living room in Walton Goggins’s home in Newly introduced York’s Hudson Valley.

The grand Victorian, simple Colonial, and traditional farmhouse-style homes scattered across upstate New York are a common subject for Kate Jordan’s lens. Her shots of Shaker-style kitchens and cozy living rooms depict all the warmth and familiarity they were designed to exude.

Industry observers note that join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more.

The city takes center stage in this Newly introduced York apartment.

Long shadows and glimpses through windows give Joseph Kramm’s interiors a palpable sense of depth. His work with galleries including The Future Perfect and Hostler Burrows also makes him well versed in giving collectible furniture its moment.

One of the most versatile interior photographers in the Northeast, Jared Kuzia captures residential projects up and down the Eastern Seaboard for architects, interior designers, and publications. Whether shooting urban apartments or coastal cabins, he is motivated by “conveying the essence of home,” as he puts it.

A bedroom in Isabella Rosselini’s converted barn on Long Island by architect Pietro Cicognani.

Francesco Lagnese’s interiors work moves comfortably between a spare, sunlit corner and the layered rooms of Tom Scheerer, Williams Lawrence, and Veere Grenney. Working between Latest York, Palm Beach, and all over Europe from his base in Munich, his itinerary extends well beyond the living room, as he also shoots architecture, portraits, and travel.

With an instantly recognizable, highly atmospheric style that’s won favor with top designers and stylists, William Jess Laird is consistently in high demand. His calm, minimal photos appear regularly in AD and many other leading art and design publications.

Olivia Palermo’s Upcoming York apartment.

According to recent reports, people are part of the picture in David Land’s photographs, from children playing in a living room to a family gathered on the sofa. In his images of work by Danielle Colding, Nina Barnieh-Blair, and more, color and everyday activity make these interiors feel welcoming, with life happening inside them.

A high-contrast interior captured by Heami Lee.

Sources indicate that there’s something innately playful about the images Lee captures for clients. Whether shooting still lifes for Edie Parker or Design Within Reach, Brooklyn-based Lee creates work that is undeniably cool.

Tour a Josh Greene–designed Upper East Side family home with a tented room.

In a recent development, capturing lived-in interiors in an authentically stunning demeanor is Tim Lenz’s calling card. The talent has shot the work of AD100 studio Carrier and Company, Hendricks Churchill, and Augusta Hoffman.

A den on the top floor of a home in Provincetown, Massachusetts, designed by Stanton Schwartz Design Group.

Consider Sean Litchfield’s portfolio a love letter to Fresh England. Maine lake houses, Cape Cod cottages, and Boston brownstones—his portfolio makes room for both rustic intimacy and a more polished setting with Nina Campbell, Patrick Ahearn, and Erin Gates included.

The dining room in Rachel Brosnahan’s apartment, which the actress designed with Zoë Feldman.

It has been revealed that pernille Loof’s restrained compositions give texture, color, and shadow room to register. A minimalist sensibility runs through her interiors and still lifes, bringing a crispness to the frame without stripping away the warmth of the subject.

A living room in Birmingham, Alabama, by Georgette Sturam Design.

According to recent reports, adam Kane Macchia’s balanced room views keep architectural features clearly legible, highlighting everything from ceiling beams to the rhythm of tall windows. His portfolio is particularly useful for designers seeking photographs that show how furnishings and a home’s bones work together.

Interior campaign for Bed Threads.

Meghan Marin photographs residential spaces as she finds them: unmade beds, displays of collected items, tables laid for dinner—all the idiosyncrasies of which bring rawness and authenticity to her shots, even if they’ve been styled to appear that way.

Step inside Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s freshly renovated Fifth Avenue family home.

Sources indicate that if the name Kelly Marshall isn’t immediately familiar, surely her contrast-rich photography—seen regularly in the pages of AD—will ring a bell. Marshall, who’s a member of the Female Design Council as well as the Black Artists + Designers Guild, is based in New York.

Designer Sara Story’s New York City living room.

Joshua McHugh’s interests extend from private residences to museums and artists’ historic homes, including those of Carlo Mollino and Wharton Esherick. His portfolio is an appealing resource for designers whose interiors put architecture, art, and objects in conversation.

Creative dream team Murdock Solon Architects and designer David Cafiero lovingly injected whimsy and joy across all four floors of a Newly introduced York City family home.

A cover star, Read McKendree’s lively interiors have fronted issues of Elle Decoration Germany, House Beautiful, and Luxe, as well as catalogs for Serena & Lily. We also love his portraits of artists at work in their studios.

Inside a Minneapolis home decadently designed by Prospect Refuge Studio.

Industry observers note that chris Mottalini’s aim each time he photographs a home is to create a portrait of the space and its occupants, revealing what’s hidden beneath the surface. His recent projects include the photography for interior designer Nina Freudenberger’s book Mountain House.

A loggia in the Moroccan home of writer and gardener Umberto Pasti.

Ngoc Minh Ngo’s images of gardens feel enveloping, with layered foliage and paths that draw the eye into the landscape. The Fresh York photographer and author’s botanical photography brings the same attention to a single bloom, making her a natural fit for projects where planting matters. In her images of landscapes by Miranda Brooks and Dan Pearson, every leaf feels considered.

Tour fashion designer Adam Lippes’s bucolic Berkshires home.

Growing up around creative matriarchs—her mother a weaver and her grandmother a painter—Isabel Parra understands the importance of an artisan’s tool kit. Her devices of choice? Natural light and its emotive shadow play and honest interior compositions. No wonder she’s caught the attention of fashion designer Adam Lippes, Oomph Home, House & Garden UK, AD, and others.

Julianne Moore’s Manhattan apartment.

Natural light, analogue photography, and a sense of intimate nostalgia guide Clément Pascal’s work—with vintage cars making occasional cameos. The view from Kelly Behun’s Manhattan apartment.

Interior at Lefay Resort and Spa.

Working out of Newly introduced York and Paris, Arrow (Sharon) Radisch’s clients include luxury brands like Gucci and Chanel, as well as editorial outlets like Cereal, for whom she shot Le Corbusier’s Paris apartment.

Inside an AD digital editor’s light-filled Maine abode.

It has been revealed that tara Rice takes a photo-journalistic approach to her work, whether in the forests or on the shorelines of Maine or across the far-reaching corners of the world. Her photography is fueled by curiosity about people and places, and the varied ways in which they overlap.

Inside a couple’s Brooklyn townhouse.

Newly introduced York. Los Angeles. Mexico City. Barcelona. Pia Riverola’s work locales read like a very appealing itinerary. Limewash paint brings emotion to an otherwise quiet interior.

Life and movement appear in full focus throughout the varied portfolio of Julia Robbs, whose work in fashion and beauty photography naturally translates over to interiors. The lifestyle component of the home, and how its occupants use it, is key to her vibrant aesthetic.

Sources indicate that A beloved portraitist, Reid Rolls started his career shooting album covers for record labels. The California native, who now lives in Brooklyn, also photographs fashion, travel, ad campaigns, and, of course, interiors, including his atmospheric images of Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s home in Charlotte for AD.

An aquatic-themed bathroom in an 1840s townhouse in Brooklyn, New York, designed by Charlap Hyman & Herrero with murals and mosaics by Lukas Geronimas Giniotis and Allison Eden Studios.

Industry observers note that from established businesses to young brands, Tori Sikkema will not only photograph your projects, she’ll also support your branding through consultations that will tailor her shoots to meet specific needs and goals. I Found the 11 Best Running Shoes for Women for Every Type of Run

  • It has been revealed that as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever. From 5Ks to marathons, lots of women are lacing up to go for a run and getting all the physical and mental health benefits that come with it. Data suggests running is great for everything from cardiovascular fitness to a healthier mindset, and it may even lower your risk of eight major diseases, making it a solid fitness habit to get into. And then there’s the fact that running makes you feel like you’ve accomplished something amazing (because you have).

It has been revealed that as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too. The best running shoes for women provide support and cushioning, with the perfect level of fit to help you forget about your footwear while you run.

In a recent development, while you can skimp on some fitness gear, a quality pair of running shoes is an important investment, according to Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois “I am very much in the camp of paying for a really good pair of running shoes,” she says. “It can help really minimize injury in the future.” (Still, if you’re on a tight budget or just want to save a buck, these are our favorite cheap running shoes.).

But, before taking the plunge on racking up miles, it’s important to figure out what kind of heel-to-toe drop, toe box, stability, cushioning, and heel stack is best for you. Finding the perfect running shoes involves understanding how specific design elements impact your comfort, performance, and overall experience.

There is no right or wrong, as everyone has different needs (and those needs for running shoes differ from walking shoes), but we'll go over the most important factors to consider when shopping for running shoes.

Recent findings suggest that hoka does it right when it comes to a durable, high-quality shoe—specifically the Clifton 11, which was released in July 2026 in tandem with the higher-performance-oriented Clifton Pro. The Clifton family has been a crowd pleaser in the running community and amongst WH editors for a long time, and with good reason.

Industry observers note that the Clifton 11 is considered one of the brand’s most versatile running shoes, making it a good fit for everyone from beginners to seasoned pros. WH style editor Shannon Zitz claims her feet never felt fatigued while she was testing this shoe, even with plantar fasciitis. “There’s technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely noticed it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running,” she says.

Industry observers note that the Clifton 11 has an eight-millimeter heel-to-toe drop to help alleviate pressure on the plantar fascia, and the brand shaved off almost half an ounce from the weight of the model’s previous version, the Clifton 10, primarily through weight-saving revisions to the shoe’s upper. This was the primary change, with Hoka keeping the midsole that we know and love the same.

These shoes offer maximum cushioning you’ll feel—the same EVA foam found in the Bondi 9 without the extra bulk. Just be aware that these don’t offer any stability innovations for flat feet, which is especially essential if you’re prone to overpronation. As for fit, the toe box does run narrow, but luckily, wide sizing is available.

Read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro.

On has built an empire out of its highly cushioned Cloudmonster line. But its most cushioned shoe of all is the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, an impressively bouncy sneaker that’ll make you feel like a gazelle bounding down the street.

It has been revealed that it’s generally accepted that the more cushioning a shoe has, the heavier its weight (because of all that foam packed into the midsole). But the On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper manages to deliver a highly cushioned shoe in a relatively lightweight 7.5 oz package. The result is a next-level energy return that feels like it’s propelling you forward with each step.

In a recent development, this sneaker has a soft, breathable upper to minimize foot sweat, along with a highly padded heel collar that lowers the risk of rubbing. I’ve worn a lot of running shoes, and that heel collar may be the thickest I’ve ever seen. There’s a nice, roomy toe box, too.

In a recent development, while there’s a lot to love about the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, it’s not perfect. This shoe’s $220 price tag puts it out of reach for many, and the tongue is on the thin side (not a deal-breaker, but some people prefer something more padded). Still, if you have the budget for it and like to feel like you’re running on actual clouds, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best On Walking Shoes.

Recent findings suggest that think of a daily trainer as the chameleon of the running shoe world. This sneaker needs to be able to be durable enough for regular use, comfortable, and versatile enough to handle higher mileage along with speedier runs. The Adidas Adizero Evo SL was designed with all of that in mind, serving up a highly adaptable shoe that works for nearly everyone. That’s probably why this shoe keeps landing on the feet of runners all over the place.

The Adizero Evo SL has a soft, bouncy feel underfoot and plenty of energy return thanks to Adidas’ proprietary Lightstrike Pro foam packed into the midsole. It’s also relatively lightweight, clocking in at just under 8 oz. The shoe’s peppy sensation and slight rocker shape support your stride but don’t push you forward in a way that feels unnatural.

In a recent development, this sneaker has an engineered mesh upper to let your feet breathe, even when you’re clocking some serious mileage. This shoe has a slightly tapered toe box, which isn’t for everyone. The outsole is also a little flat and isn’t the grippiest you’ll find, but road runners are unlikely to have an glitch. While you’re probably not choosing a running shoe based on looks alone, it doesn’t hurt that the Adizero Evo SL looks sleek.

It has been revealed that the best shoe for recovery runs is a total workhorse, delivering enough stability and cushioning to keep you comfortable as you move along at a moderate pace. The Brooks Ghost Max 3 is up for the challenge, with a wide, stable base and supportive feel to take the pressure off your joints.

Sources indicate that this isn’t a stability shoe, per se—it won’t work to correct your stride—but it still creates a sense like you’re not going to roll an ankle or have any other gait problems as you pound the pavement. The Ghost Max 3 is a heavier shoe, although I haven’t noticed any fatigue or extra drag in it. But this sneaker holds up well to high-volume running. I wear this regularly and have never noticed any durability issues.

Industry observers note that the Ghost Max 3 features nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam for support and cushioning. However, it won’t give you a sinking-in feel and there is limited energy return, which could be a pro or con, depending on what you’re after. This sneaker also has a jacquard mesh upper that feels a little softer than many other running shoes out there. The Ghost Max 3 provides plenty of room, from the midfoot to the toe box, making it a good fit for people with wider feet. Just don’t initiative to do any speed work in this shoe—it’s a little too heavy for that.

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

Recent findings suggest that it's clear that Lululemon’s Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There’s a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you’re going down.

Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that’s pretty common in a trail shoe, and it got better with time and more wear.

Read More: Best Trail Running Shoes.

There’s a wide range of shoes that consider themselves “stability” sneakers, but the Hoka Arahi 8 does a solid job correcting your stride with each step without being annoying. Many stability shoes are clunky and heavy, but the Arahi 8 manages to be lightweight at just 7.7 oz.

The Arahi 8 features a lot of changes from the previous version, the Arahi 7. This shoe uses special H-frame technology, featuring foam at the inner and outer foot, to deliver a more balanced support system. It’s roomy and comfortable, too. But this shoe is clearly not for everyone.

It has been revealed that the level of stability is high, and that constant gait correction may feel like too much for some people. It also isn’t very responsive, so you’re not getting much back from your shoe with each stride other than security. (To be fair, though, that’s what people are usually after with a stability shoe.) Still, the Arahi 8 is impressively cushioned and very comfortable, whether you’re working your way through a long training session or just going out on a daily run.

According to recent reports, long runs require plenty of cushioning to support you along the way. The Nike Vomero Plus, which won the award for Best Cushioned Running Shoe in the 2026 Women’s Health Fitness Awards, is here to help. This shoe delivers a fun, bouncy feel that helps propel you as you rack up the miles.

The Vomero Plus has a roomy toe box and overall comfortable feel, serving up a shoe that makes long runs a little more seamless. That bounciness comes courtesy of Nike’s ZoomX foam, which is positioned along the length of the shoe. The engineered upper is crafted from yarn for a soft, breathable sensation.

The Vomero Plus provides a grippy outsole, making it perfect for the pavement. But if you’re looking for a stability shoe, the Vomero Plus isn’t it. Its high heel stack and bounciness is too much for that. But if you want a highly cushioned feel as you log some serious miles, this is an excellent choice.

The right race day shoe has the tough challenge of being supportive, cushiony, and lightweight, helping you to hit a PR without feeling like your footwear is holding you back. The Newly introduced Balance FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5 is designed with longer-distance racers (think: half and marathon runners) in mind, but can still be an excellent choice for 5Ks and 10Ks thanks to its lightweight (6 oz) construction and solid energy return.

It has been revealed that let’s get this out of the way now: At $265, this is not a cheap shoe. With that, it’s unlikely to be a good investment for the occasional racer. But if your weekends are booked with road races, it’s worth at least considering.

This shoe delivers a locked-in feel, along with great traction to give you more confidence, even over wet surfaces. The roomy toe box and breathable upper also reinforce the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5’s comfortable feel. This shoe is stable without sacrificing punchiness, helping you to feel supported as you stride. Just be aware that the midfoot and heel may feel a little too narrow for those with wider feet. But, luckily, this sneaker is available in wide widths, too.

Read More: Best Running Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis.

It has been revealed that the lululemon Beyondfeel running shoes truly live up to their name. They’re comfortable at the heels (and everywhere), with a heel stack that provides just the right amount of cushioning. It absorbs impact while still feeling responsive, especially during long runs. Plus, the cushioning around the ankle delivers security in every step.

The heel-to-toe drop is also a game changer—it really makes a difference for runners who heel-strike. Instead of feeling the usual jarring sensation from heel-striking, there are smooth transitions from each step. The bounce in the heel also makes it easier to maintain a steady stride without losing momentum, which is a huge benefit for runners who naturally land on their heels. The shoes guide feet to strike with the midfoot instead of the heel.

Industry observers note that these shoes feel slightly bouncy while you run, and offer decent grip for trails and roads, making for a versatile running shoe. If you’re an overpronator, this isn’t the shoe for you—it doesn’t provide enough medial support (on the inside of the shoe). But it’s got plenty of features to make running a dream for heel strikers.

Read More: Best lululemon Shoes Ranked.

Industry observers note that there’s a range in severity with overpronators, and what works for one won’t work for everyone. But the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 does a solid job trying to please everyone in the overpronation camp. This shoe delivers a feel that’s not too soft or too firm, giving you the support and stability you need without feeling like you’re in a “special” shoe.

This shoe is lightweight for a stability shoe at 8.5 oz, making it good for most runs that don’t involve speed work. It also delivers a solid, locked-in sensation to make you feel secure with each step. The shoe’s OrthoLite sockliner also supports that cozier feel. The Gel-Nimbus 28 feels slightly springy underfoot, which is rare for a stability shoe. (Still, the overall effect isn’t very responsive compared to non-stability shoes.).

In a recent development, asics in general tends to run narrow and the Gel-Nimbus 28 is no exception. If your feet tend to teeter between regular and wide sizes, you may want to consider hedging your bets and trying out a larger size.

The best shoe for speed work is very different from what you need for distance training or even race day. The Saucony Endorphin Azura is a lightweight (7.5 oz) shoe with a snappy feel that still manages to make you feel stable and locked in as you zip around.

Recent findings suggest that the Saucony Endorphin Azura uses Pebax foam to create a responsive, bouncy feel, making you feel a little faster than usual. It also has a wide and stable base for added security during training. While it’s designed for speed, you can still comfortably wear this sneaker for longer runs and daily mileage. Just be aware that the shoe’s special SpeedRoll technology may feel slightly awkward at slower speeds.

The Endorphin Azura’s outsole features XT-900 rubber for a grippy feel underfoot, making you feel comfortable pushing the pace. Saucony shoes are known for a narrower fit, and the Endorphin Azura is no exception. If you have wider feet, it may be best to look elsewhere. (It unfortunately doesn’t come in wide sizes.).

Maximum Cushioning: This type of cushion feels amazingly plush and has excellent shock absorption, which is essential for long-distance running. While they’re designed to minimize the impact on the joints, they’re not the best for speed workouts unless the shoe has a lower heel-to-toe drop and some firmness.

Medium: If you want to balance speed with stability, medium cushioning is ideal. Too much cushioning can cause runners with flat feet to overpronate more from the bulkiness and softness. So, this type of cushioning is best if you want a more aligned gait.

In a recent development, this is the difference in height between the heel and front part (known as the forefoot) of the shoe. It can impact how your foot lands on the ground when you run. Low drops (0 to 4 mm) are flatter and encourage a natural running style where you land in the middle or front of your foot. They’re great if you like to feel close to the ground, enjoy trail running, or prefer a minimalist shoe design. Medium drop (5 to 8 mm) is a versatile option that offers mid-height and cushioning—this works well for most running styles. High drop (9 to 12 mm) tends to have more height in the heel to absorb impact (this is great for heel-strikers).

According to recent reports, this is the height of the cushion under the heel. It’s measured from the outsole (the bottom of the shoe) to the insole (where your foot rests). Higher stacks offer more softness for long-distance running or for those who need less impact on the joints. Prioritizing this means sacrificing ground feel, and for some, that may feel unbalanced given the additional height.

According to recent reports, running shoes can provide a slew of benefits to suit your feet, but podiatrists stress the importance of getting a well-fitting shoe. “The shoe should fit your foot well and not cause any rubbing on the toes,” says Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California “They should feel comfortable immediately upon putting them on and walking around.”.

Consider these areas of the shoe when checking the fit:.

Toe Box: This is the front part of the shoe where the toes sit. Toes spread naturally when you have extra room in the toe box, and this is especially important during long runs since feet can swell. But if the toe box is too big, it can lead to sliding and instability in the shoes.

Sources indicate that length: Since feet often swell from pounding pavement, it’s a good idea to have about a thumb’s width away from the tip of the shoe to your toe. If you’re unsure of your size, the best bet is to visit a running store to get properly fitted.

Sources indicate that arch Support: Those with flat feet and overpronators (when your foot lands on your outside heel and rolls inward) will want to look for shoes with enough firmness and high arch support to help keep feet aligned. Too much cushioning can create an unbalanced feeling, which can further aggravate pain. Those with neutral to high arches will have no complications wearing shoes with neutral support. Most shoes specify which arch type they accommodate, so make sure to read their product descriptions. And, definitely don’t wear shoes with no arch support—your feet need support.

The type of running workouts you strategy to do will dictate elements like cushioning, support, and weight. More cushioning is often better with daily training and distance runs. You may also get away with a slightly heavier (but not too heavy) shoe, which usually means there’s more cushioning and stability. But shoes for speed work and race day tend to have less cushioning and a lighter weight, making it easier to move faster. For a deep-dive into the topic of running shoe selection, check out our story about how to figure out which type of running shoe you need.

A stability shoe can help correct gait challenges like overpronation, which is when your foot rolls inward excessively when you run or walk. Not everyone needs a stability shoe, but some level of stability is important for reducing injury risk when you’re an overpronator. There are a few ways to tell if you overpronate, per Graves: Your feet appear to be rolling inward when you stand in a relaxed position and the heels of shoes you’ve worn are tilted inward.

It has been revealed that you should switch out your running shoes every 300 to 500 miles. An easy way to maximize your shoe lifespan is to have a few pairs that you rotate between runs. Also, if you visually see them degrading, it's time to snag a fresh pair.

It has been revealed that running shoes can be washed in cold water in the washing machine with light detergent, or spot-cleaned with a sponge. But, you should never put your shoes in the dryer—they can shrink! Instead, let them air dry in the sun.

A simple at-home way to determine your arch type is the wet footprint test. You simply dip your foot in the water and step onto paper. If you see your entire foot, you have flat feet. Your foot will look like a comma if you have high arches, while a neutral arch will show slight elevation.

I’ve tested dozens of pairs of running shoes to determine which make the cut for the best running shoes for women. As a personal trainer, fitness writer, and runner with years of experience testing running shoes, I put each pair to the test during two-mile runs where I evaluated key performance factors such as cushioning, stability, comfort, support, traction, and responsiveness. I also considered how well the shoes supported my stride and whether or not they helped me maintain a consistent pace. Additionally, WH fitness editors provided feedback on select shoes they love to wear during training and racing.

Recent findings suggest that they jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada.

Interior by Marie-Anne Derville.

Recent findings suggest that born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and right now living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life.

A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.

With Harry Nuriev, Festen, and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture.

The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams.

According to recent reports, henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke.

A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill.

Helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality.

The Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators.

Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment.

Sources indicate that partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio, Nilufar Gallery, and JW Anderson among their clients. A villa in New Zealand by Patterson Associates.

Joseph Dirand’s Paris apartment.

Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios.

Having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris.

Industry observers note that A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators.

Inside the Paris apartment of Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, as seen in AD France.

The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan.

A kitchen by AKB Design in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec.

The reception room of the barn on designer Jean-Louis Denoit’s watercress farm in France.

Designer Meg Sharpe turns a traditional warren of rooms into an airy idyll where livability and flair are winsome bedfellows.

The Paris apartment belonging to Gregoire Marot and Thomas Dupré de St Maur, designed with help of their friend the designer Eric Allart.

The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use
